question: A weight-loss advert under a dramatic before-and-after photo. Which line did US regulators decide no longer excuses it?
answer: Results not typical. In 2009 the US Federal Trade Commission revised its endorsement guides: an advert showing an extraordinary result must also say what typical users achieve. Shown someone who lost 40 kg, readers take it as the norm, and a line of small print does not undo a big photograph.
move: A vivid single case speaks louder than the small print beside it.
ask: Which success story am I measuring myself against that was never typical?

scene.head: Weight-loss advert
scene.title: Real people, real results
scene.body: I lost 40 kg and never felt hungry. Real customer, real story. *Results not typical. Individual results may vary.

phrases.plain: One customer, picked from many, lost 40 kg
phrases.why: The best case is chosen for being extraordinary. That is what makes it look ordinary.

phrases.plain: True for her; it says nothing about you
phrases.why: A real story can still be a rare one.

phrases.plain: Most buyers lose far less; we won't say how much
phrases.why: Since 2009 the FTC has wanted the typical result shown, not just this line.
Vary sounds even-handed. With the best case shown, it can only vary downwards.

scene.ask: One line tries to undo the photograph. Which?
scene.watch: When an advert shows its best case, ask what the typical buyer got.

reference: US Federal Trade Commission, Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising, 16 CFR Part 255, 2009
